topic.title: SHA-256 vs SHA-1: why SHA-1 is no longer considered secure

post.title: SHA-256 vs SHA-1: Why SHA-1 Is No Longer Secure
post.description: SHA-256 is the safer choice: SHA-1 has practical collision attacks, letting two different files share one hash. Here is how they differ, with code.

body.text: SHA-256 is the better choice for anything new. It produces a 256-bit digest, and no practical collision attacks are publicly known against it. SHA-1 produces a 160-bit digest, and researchers have built two different files that share the same SHA-1 hash, so it should not be used where an attacker could influence the input.

You can generate SHA-1 and SHA-256 hashes for any text in the [Hash Generator](/hash-generator) and compare the output directly. The tool runs in your browser, which matters if you are hashing tokens or other secrets.
SHA-256 vs SHA-1 at a glance

items: Output size: SHA-1 is 160 bits, shown as 40 hex characters. SHA-256 is 256 bits, shown as 64 hex characters.
Collision resistance: SHA-1 collisions are practical to produce. No practical SHA-256 collision is publicly known.
Standards status: NIST has deprecated SHA-1 for digital signatures. SHA-256 is widely recommended for new designs.
Speed: SHA-1 is somewhat faster, but the difference rarely matters in real workloads, so it is not a good reason to choose it.
Encoding: both are usually printed as hex, but base64 output is shorter. See [Base64 vs Base64URL](/blog/base64-vs-base64url-differences-when-to-use) if you need to pick one.

body.text: Why SHA-1 is considered broken

A hash function is supposed to make it infeasible to find two different inputs with the same digest. This is called collision resistance. For a 160-bit hash, a generic birthday attack needs roughly 2^80 work, which is far too much for practical use.

In 2017, Google and CWI Amsterdam published the SHAttered attack. It found a SHA-1 collision using about 2^63 operations, far below the generic bound. The researchers released two different PDF files with identical SHA-1 hashes.

The practical risk comes from who controls the input. If an attacker can supply one of the two files, they can craft a malicious file that carries the same hash as a trusted one. That affects code signing, certificate signing, download verification and any system that uses a hash as proof that content has not changed.

Some version control systems and protocols still rely on SHA-1 by default, and their maintainers have been working on SHA-256 support. If you run into SHA-1 in a file format or protocol you do not control, you may need to match it, but that is an interoperability decision, not a reason to pick SHA-1 for new code.
Generate both hashes in code
In Node.js, the built-in crypto module supports both algorithms. The input below is the ASCII string hello, with no trailing newline.

aaf4c61ddcc5e8a2dabede0f3b482cd9aea9434d
2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824
In Python, hashlib does the same job:

import hashlib

data = b'hello'
print(hashlib.sha1(data).hexdigest())
print(hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest())
On Linux, you can hash a string from the shell with printf. Avoid echo here, because it adds a newline and changes the hash:
printf 'hello' | sha256sum
On macOS, use shasum -a 256 instead of sha256sum.
Pitfalls that cause wrong hashes

items: A trailing newline changes the result. echo 'hello' hashes hello plus a newline. Use printf or strip the newline before hashing.
Hash bytes, not characters. UTF-8 is the usual choice. The same string encoded as UTF-16 produces a different digest.
Compare like with like. A hex digest and a base64 digest of the same bytes look different but match when decoded.
The empty string has a fixed SHA-256 digest, e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855. If you see this value, your code is probably hashing an empty input by mistake.

body.text: Choosing the right hash

items: Verifying a download: do not rely on a checksum published on the same page as the file. An attacker who can replace the download can often replace the checksum too, and the same is true for SHA-256. Instead, get the checksum or a signature through a separate trusted channel, such as a signed release announcement or a package manager's signed metadata. Better still, verify a cryptographic signature (for example GPG or a code-signing signature) made with a key you already trust.
New digital signatures or fingerprints: use SHA-256 or a longer SHA-2 variant such as SHA-384 or SHA-512.
Message authentication: use HMAC, not a bare hash of a key concatenated with a message. In Node.js: crypto.createHmac('sha256', key).update(message).digest('hex').
Password storage: do not use any plain hash, SHA-256 included, because it is too fast to resist guessing. Use a password hashing function such as Argon2, scrypt or bcrypt from a well-tested library.
Matching an existing system: use the algorithm the other side requires, and document the risk if that algorithm is SHA-1.

body.text: FAQ
Is SHA-1 still safe for checksums?

For catching accidental corruption, SHA-1 still detects most random errors. The problem is tampering: if someone can alter the file and the checksum, SHA-1 no longer gives you a reliable guarantee. Use SHA-256 for checksums you publish or rely on, and deliver the checksum through a channel the attacker cannot change.
Is SHA-256 the same as SHA-2?
SHA-256 is one member of the SHA-2 family, which also includes SHA-224, SHA-384 and SHA-512. SHA-3 is a separate design, not a successor that replaces SHA-2.
Why is a SHA-256 hash 64 characters long?
A SHA-256 digest is 256 bits. Each hex character represents 4 bits, so 256 divided by 4 gives 64 characters.
Should I switch existing SHA-1 data to SHA-256?

If the SHA-1 values protect against tampering, yes: plan a migration and recompute with SHA-256 where you control both sides. If they only detect accidental changes or serve as internal cache keys, the urgency is lower.

review.title_ko: SHA-256 vs SHA-1: SHA-1이 더 이상 안전하지 않은 이유
summary_ko: SHA-256이 새로운 용도에 더 나은 선택이며, 공개적으로 알려진 실용적 충돌 공격이 없다고 설명합니다.
SHA-1은 2017년 SHAttered 공격으로 같은 해시를 가진 서로 다른 두 PDF 파일을 만들 수 있음이 입증되었으며, 공격자가 입력을 통제할 수 있을 때 코드 서명, 인증서, 다운로드 검증 등에 위험합니다.
Node.js(crypto), Python(hashlib), Linux/macOS 셸에서 SHA-1과 SHA-256 해시를 생성하는 코드와 명령을 제공하며, 'hello'의 해시 값도 포함합니다.
흔한 실수로 끝의 줄바꿈 포함(echo 대신 printf 사용), 문자 인코딩 차이, 16진수와 base64 비교, 빈 문자열의 SHA-256 값을 들고 있습니다.
용도별 선택 가이드로 다운로드 검증(별도 신뢰 채널 또는 서명 사용), HMAC, 비밀번호 저장(Argon2/scrypt/bcrypt), 기존 시스템 호환성을 다룹니다.
FAQ에서 SHA-1 체크섬의 한계, SHA-2 계열 관계, SHA-256 길이 계산, 기존 데이터 마이그레이션 판단을 설명합니다.
applied: "Verifying a download: use the SHA-256 published by the vendor. Do not trust a SHA-1 checksum from the same page as the file, since an attacker who can alter the download may alter the checksum too." 이 문장은 SHA-256 체크섬이 같은 페이지에 있으면 안전하다는 잘못된 인상을 준다. 공격자가 다운로드를 바꿀 수 있다면 같은 페이지의 SHA-256 값도 바꿀 수 있으므로, 알고리즘과 무관하게 같은 채널의 체크섬은 신뢰할 수 없다.
